README.md documents both commands and the reason. agent/scripts/verify/KN-089.mjs: 6 checks green, including a positive control that the detector can see the browser that IS installed here, so a detector hard-wired to "missing" cannot pass. Four mutations, all caught: setup:browsers dropping `chromium` (installs three browsers, one configured); README losing the command; the browser check moved to the END of KN-003; KN-003 dropping chromiumStatus entirely. A fifth mutation rewrote the check's human label and broke a check that had no business caring, so that check was rewritten to locate the browser check by its `chromiumStatus(` call instead. Gate green: lint 0 warnings, tsc 0 errors, 438 tests (4 graphql, 333 web, 101 api), build 227ms, schema.gql matches the resolvers.

tasks.title: Stop AppProviders mutating the lingui singleton during render
tasks.desc: AppProviders calls i18n.activate(locale) in the render body, guarded by a locale comparison. Under concurrent rendering React can render a subtree, mutate the singleton, then abandon that render, leaving a committed tree reading the wrong catalog. Two providers mounted at once, which a Storybook Docs page does, share the same singleton and whichever renders last wins for both. The dir and lang effect on document.documentElement has the same last-writer-wins problem and no cleanup. Give each provider its own I18n instance, or move activation into a store React can subscribe to.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major and the analysis is correct. It was written this way to avoid a flash of the previous language, which an effect does cause, so the fix has to keep synchronous activation without mutating shared state during render. It matters as soon as anything renders two locales at once, which the Docs page and any side-by-side comparison do.
tasks.exit: A story that mounts a Persian and an English AppProviders side by side renders each in its own language and direction, the switch still shows no flash of the previous catalog, and a test covers both.

Create the structure, move the prose, wire the Docs pages to read it, and write the guard.

Prose in a TSX is prose only the person editing the file sees, in one language, and the product is bilingual by rule: a Docs page that is English at the top and Persian once you scroll is the failure mode AGENTS.md section 5 names.
tasks.exit: src/shared/story-docs/en and fa exist and carry the prose for every story, no .tsx under src holds a docblock above const meta or a story export, the Docs pages render the markdown in the toolbar language, and a guard test fails when a prop or a story is missing from either language.
notes: CONFIRMED AGAIN by a roast on KN-006: LanguageSwitch.tsx carries its component documentation as a JSDoc block and src/shared/story-docs does not exist, so the contract is now broken by two components rather than one. The card is unchanged; this is evidence it should be worked before the component queue rather than after, since every component added meanwhile is another one to migrate.

tasks.title: Enforce the import conventions with a lint rule, and fix what already breaks them
tasks.desc: AGENTS.md requires MUI from the top-level barrel only, absolute src/... imports with no relative parent imports, and an index.ts barrel in every folder with more than one file. apps/web violates all three throughout: every component deep-imports @mui/material/Box, AppProviders reaches up through ../i18n and ../theme/rtl, and there are no barrels. Deep MUI imports were once a bundle-size trick and are now just an inconsistency, and a relative parent import breaks the moment a file moves. This matters most NOW, before the component queue: 30 component folders written the wrong way is a rename nobody wants, and the convention only holds if the lint holds it.

tasks.title: Stop a later scoped ESLint block silently re-exempting a lingui hole
tasks.desc: ESLint replaces rule options rather than merging them, so a config block added later and scoped to part of the tree, say src/shared/**, can reconfigure lingui/no-unlocalized-strings with aria-label exempt for those files only. Every existing check would still pass: the fixtures live in src/gate-fixtures and would keep failing, and KN-087s config check reads the shared options constant, which the override does not touch. Check the RESOLVED configuration instead, with ESLint calculateConfigForFile over a sample of paths across the tree, and require the same exemption list everywhere.

It is also how the last two holes got in, once as a name and once as a shape, so the third will arrive as a scope.

tasks.title: The token-name value exemption reaches aria-label and title
tasks.desc: The lingui rule ignores any value matching ^[a-z-]+/[a-z0-9-/]+$, added so a token name rendered as a label, bg/page, would pass. It applies to EVERY value, so aria-label="delete/application" and title="delete/application" both pass, verified by probe. Scope the exemption to where token names actually appear rather than to every string in the codebase, or drop it and localise the Foundations story labels.

The pattern across all three is an exemption written for one legitimate case that quietly covers every case, and the fix has to narrow the SCOPE rather than the pattern, or a fourth shape will be found.
tasks.exit: aria-label="delete/application" and title="delete/application" both fail npm run lint, a committed fixture holds both, the Foundations token story still passes, and agent/scripts/verify/KN-087.mjs requires the fixture by name.

KN-087.mjs lints the fixture by name and KN-003.mjs requires it by name. agent/scripts/verify/KN-094.mjs, 8 checks green: the fixture holds both; both fail on the lingui rule; THE MUTATION, restoring the exemption makes the fixture lint clean (exit 0), so it fails BECAUSE of the removal; the pattern is absent from the config with comments stripped; the whole workspace lints; the Foundations token story passes (vitest storybook src/theme); hiding the fixture makes KN-087 fail naming it; KN-003's required array names it. Four mutations, all caught on the check that names each: fixture loses its title export; exemption restored for good; KN-087 stops linting the fixture while still naming it in its other list (MISSED by the first version, which grepped the name anywhere in KN-087's source, so that check now runs KN-087 instead); KN-003's entry commented out. Two defects in my own verifier found on the way: the in-check mutation used String.replace with a replacement containing $', which pastes the rest of the file, so ESLint crashed and the check blamed the fixture; and its failure message guessed at causes it could not see. Both fixed. KN-003.mjs full gate green, 11 checks, every planted unlocalized string failing; KN-087.mjs green. No UI changed, so there is nothing to open in a browser.

tasks.title: The stories-only title exemption covers every JSX title, not just meta.title
tasks.desc: The lingui block for *.stories.tsx exempts the property name title so a story meta can carry its sidebar path, App/Shell. ESLint matches the NAME wherever it appears, so <Box title="Delete this application" /> inside a story also passes, verified by probe, and that renders a real tooltip in Storybook. Exempt the meta object specifically, by shape or by position, rather than the property name across the whole file.

tasks.exit: A story containing <Box title="Delete this application" /> fails npm run lint while the same file keeps its meta title App/Shell, a committed fixture holds both, and agent/scripts/verify/KN-087.mjs requires it by name.
tasks.evidence: The stories-only lingui block, which exempted the NAME title, is removed; stories are linted by the src block like any screen. A meta title passes by TYPE: StoryMeta (src/shared/story-docs/story-meta.ts) narrows it to the union of the seven registered story paths, and useTsTypes skips a literal typed as a union of string literals. All seven metas now satisfy StoryMeta. src/gate-fixtures/unlocalized-story-title.stories.tsx renders <Box title="Delete this application" /> beside a meta title App/Shell; eslint reports exactly one lingui error, on the JSX title line, none on the meta title. agent/scripts/verify/KN-095.mjs, 9 checks green, with two mutations inside it: re-adding a stories block that exempts title by name makes the fixture pass (so it tests the name), and retyping the fixture's meta with plain Meta adds an error on the meta title (so the title passes BECAUSE of its type; App/Shell contains a p, so the KN-214 flag bug cannot whitelist it by accident). Storybook's glob now excludes src/gate-fixtures: a build indexes 39 entries from the 7 real story files and not the fixture; the control build with the old glob indexed 40 including it. The docs guard's glob mirrors the exclusion. Hiding the fixture makes KN-087 fail naming it; KN-003's required list names it. Gate: KN-003.mjs green (lint, tsc, suite with 100 percent coverage, both builds, every planted unlocalized string failing), KN-087.mjs green, storybook project 32 of 32 stories in 7 files. Two defects in my own verifier fixed on the way: it parsed eslint JSON with npm's stderr appended, and a mutation guard refused to run because the fixture's comment mentioned StoryMeta. Filed from this work: KN-214 (critical, the no-letter ignore pattern is compiled without flags). No product UI changed.

tasks.title: A literal type alias carries an unlocalized string past the lingui rule
tasks.desc: With useTsTypes enabled, assigning a string through a literal type alias and passing the variable to a prop passes the lint: type Label = "Delete this application"; const label: Label = "Delete this application"; <IconButton aria-label={label} />. No as, no any, no suppression, so nothing else in the gate objects either. Decide whether the rule can be configured to follow it, and if it cannot, add a check that flags a literal type alias whose value is a sentence.

It matters because it is the shape a well-meaning contributor would write when trying to centralise strings, so it will arrive by accident rather than by evasion.
tasks.exit: The literal-type-alias form fails npm run lint or fails a dedicated check, a committed fixture holds it, and the check is proved by a planted break.

tasks.title: MDX story files are linted by no lingui block at all
tasks.desc: .storybook/main.ts includes ../src/**/*.mdx in its stories glob, and neither lingui block in eslint.config.js matches an .mdx file: the source block is src/**/*.{ts,tsx} and the stories block is **/*.stories.tsx. So a supported src/foo.stories.mdx can render <button aria-label="Delete this application" /> with no enforcement whatsoever. Either lint MDX with eslint-plugin-mdx and apply the rule, or stop accepting MDX in the stories glob and say so.

tasks.exit: An .mdx file under src containing a bare English aria-label fails npm run lint, or the stories glob no longer accepts .mdx and DESIGN.md or AGENTS.md records which was chosen and why; either way a committed fixture proves it.

tasks.title: Prove the STORYBOOK test project reports a failure too
tasks.desc: KN-088 proves the real unit project detects a broken test. The storybook project, which runs every story in headless Chromium and is where component behaviour is actually checked, has no such proof: its story set comes from the stories glob in .storybook/main.ts, so a fixture story needs that glob to admit it. Add a gate story with a play function that asserts something untrue, admitted only in gate mode, and require the run to report it.

If it silently ran zero stories, or swallowed a failing play function, every component task after this would report green having checked nothing, and the unit project passing would hide it. This is the same question KN-088 asks, aimed at the project that matters more.
tasks.exit: A committed story whose play function asserts something untrue is run by the real storybook project in gate mode and reported as a failure, it does not appear in an ordinary run, and emptying the stories glob makes agent/scripts/verify/KN-003.mjs fail.

tasks.title: Scope the gate run and its passing count to the unit project
tasks.desc: agent/scripts/verify/KN-003.mjs runs KARNAMA_GATE_FIXTURES=1 npm test and reads the suite-wide summary line, Tests 1 failed | N passed, which aggregates the unit and storybook projects. Only the fixture filename is project-attributed. Once the storybook project has twenty passing stories, a unit project with no ordinary tests at all satisfies every assertion. Run the gate command with --project unit, or read project-scoped structured output, so the passing count proves the unit include is populated.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical and the arithmetic is right: the twenty-passing-tests assertion is the one meant to prove the ordinary include still works, and it is the one not scoped to the project it is about. It is invisible today because there are only seven stories, and it becomes wrong silently the moment the component queue starts, which is the next thing this project does.
tasks.exit: The gate run is scoped to the unit project, emptying the unit include makes agent/scripts/verify/KN-003.mjs fail because the run reports no passing unit tests rather than because a source string changed, and the storybook project having any number of passing stories does not affect it.

tasks.title: Make the gate-fixtures flag hermetic
tasks.desc: vitest.config.ts reads Boolean(process.env.KARNAMA_GATE_FIXTURES), so any non-empty inherited value enables the deliberately failing fixture, including the string "0". agent/scripts/verify/KN-003.mjs spawns the ordinary npm test with the parent environment unchanged, so a CI job or a shell that has the variable set makes an ordinary run include a test designed to fail. Compare against the exact string "1" and scrub the variable explicitly for every run that is meant to be ordinary.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major. A flag that changes what the test suite runs is dangerous by construction, and this one turns on for a value that reads as off. The failure it produces is the worst kind: a suite that fails for a reason nobody can find, in an environment nobody thought about.
tasks.exit: KARNAMA_GATE_FIXTURES=0 npm test passes and runs no fixture, the ordinary run inside agent/scripts/verify/KN-003.mjs passes with the variable set to any value in the parent environment, and both are proved by planted environments.

fixedSince.why: The round's three findings were all the RALPH step 5 second clause, a verifier reporting success without establishing the exit condition, so all three were fixed in-task and the code changed after the review. Commit 5d97d30 is exactly that fix and nothing else. Note for anyone reading the archive: --filed none records that nothing became a CARD, not that nothing survived. All three findings were real, reproduced, and repaired here.

tasks.evidence: node agent/scripts/verify/KN-100.mjs passes, 11 checks, about 3.2 minutes. Both halves of the flag are closed. apps/web/vitest.config.ts opts in on the exact string '1', so '0', 'true', 'yes', 'false', 'no' and unset are all ordinary runs, proved by listing the resolved unit project for each and requiring failing.gate.ts absent. agent/scripts/verify/lib/child-env.mjs scrubs the key out of every child environment, matching on the uppercased key because Windows environment variables are case-insensitive while a spread of process.env is a plain object that is not. The exit condition's second clause is RUN, not approximated: KN-003 itself is spawned with an inherited '1' and must pass, 124 seconds, after an earlier version tried to satisfy that clause with a vitest list and was right to be rejected for it. Every absence is paired with a positive control on the same instrument and every listing must be non-empty first, because a listing that fails or collects nothing is indistinguishable from a correctly scrubbed one. The 'no way around it' check now counts child launches against scrubs, reading launcher names out of the child_process import, which catches a spawn with NO env option, the bypass that inherits by default and that the previous source grep passed. The anti-vacuity floor is project-scoped rather than suite-wide. Eight mutations, each caught with its own message: Boolean(env) restored, the scrub disabled, the scrub made case-sensitive, the scrub swallowing the deliberate opt-in, KN-003 reverted to a raw environment, KN-003 keeping the scrub but growing a second spawn that spreads the parent, the same with NO env option, and the unit project narrowed until it reported 3 passing tests. AGENTS section 5 items 1 to 4 all ran green inside that verify, since KN-003 runs lint, lint:tsc, the suite with coverage, build and build-storybook. Items 5 to 7 are the rendered-result checks and do not apply: this task changes no UI. What this does NOT establish, and what is already filed: the full npm test check still reads a suite-wide summary line, KN-099, so it is the project-scoped check beside it that establishes the unit project ran. The empty-string entry in the falsy-value list exercises the UNSET path on Windows rather than the empty one, which is said in the code rather than left to look like more than it is. The mutation cases live in a scratch directory and are thrown away, KN-136.

tasks.title: Run destructive mutation verifiers in an isolated worktree
tasks.desc: agent/scripts/verify/KN-088.mjs mutates apps/web/vitest.config.ts in the shared checkout and restores it in a finally block. finally does not survive SIGKILL, an interrupt, an OOM or a crash, two concurrent runs can snapshot each others broken state and restore it, and the snapshot is a UTF-8 decode and re-encode rather than the byte copy the comment claims. Copy the repository into a temporary worktree with git worktree add, mutate there, and leave the shared checkout untouched. Apply the same treatment to the scratchpad mutation scripts, which have the same shape.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major. Every verifier in this repository is documented as read-only and this one is the exception, which is exactly the file most likely to be run twice at once or interrupted. Leaving a broken config behind would be blamed on the gate rather than on the script that broke it, and that is an expensive hour.
tasks.exit: agent/scripts/verify/KN-088.mjs performs its mutation in a temporary git worktree, killing it mid-run leaves apps/web/vitest.config.ts byte-identical, and two concurrent runs both pass and leave the file byte-identical.
notes: 2026-09-10, from the KN-094 roast: agent/scripts/verify/KN-094.mjs is another instance. It writes apps/web/eslint.config.js and renames a committed fixture inside try/finally, and a killed process skips the finally. The worst leftover is the exemption restored in the config, which ordinary lint does not notice because src/gate-fixtures is ignored. Filed here rather than as a new card because it is this card's class exactly.

2026-09-10, from the KN-095 roast: agent/scripts/verify/KN-095.mjs is a third instance. It writes a stories block exempting the name title into apps/web/eslint.config.js and rewrites a committed fixture inside try/finally; a killed process leaves the exemption in place, and ordinary lint cannot see it because src/gate-fixtures is ignored.

tasks.title: The gate-fixtures README describes a file and a mechanism that no longer exist
tasks.desc: apps/web/src/gate-fixtures/README.md names failing.test.ts, which is now failing.gate.ts, says vitest excludes the directory through the config, which is now flag-controlled inclusion, and says the verifier runs the tools against "these two files", of which there are now six. Rewrite it against what is there, and add the two mechanisms it never described: gate mode, and the fixtures being required by name as well as discovered.
tasks.why: A roast rated this minor and it is the only kind of documentation that actually gets read, a README sitting in the directory it describes. A false one is worse than none, because it tells the next reader that the exclusion is in the config and they will go looking for it.
tasks.exit: Every file and mechanism the README names exists, no file in the directory is unmentioned, and a check in agent/scripts/verify/KN-003.mjs fails when a fixture is added or renamed without the README following.

tasks.title: Coverage from the storybook project is discarded for any file the unit project also touches
tasks.desc: The two vitest projects both produce v8 coverage. For a file only the browser project touches, like src/app/App.tsx, the browser numbers are reported. For a file BOTH touch, the unit project numbers win and the browser ones are lost: src/theme/useColorScheme.ts reported its hook as uncovered while every story exercises it through AppProviders. Reproduce it, then merge the two reports properly, with a per-project report to compare against so the merge can be checked rather than believed.
tasks.why: The 100 percent number is the standard this project is built around and it is currently overstated, silently, for exactly the files that have both a unit test and a story, which is what every component in the queue will be. A component whose branches are only reached from a story would read as uncovered and get a pointless unit test, or worse, someone would lower the threshold to fit.
tasks.exit: A function reached only from a story and living in a file that also has unit tests counts as covered, a per-project coverage report exists, and a planted uncovered branch in such a file fails the run.

tasks.title: Give the product a colour scheme setting that persists
tasks.desc: AppProviders takes a colorScheme preference of light, dark or system and resolves it, but nothing in the product sets it: main.tsx mounts with the default, so dark and system exist only through the Storybook toolbar. Put the choice somewhere the whole tree can reach, persist it, and give the user a control. The same shape is needed for the language switch, so build one mechanism and use it twice.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical and the reading is fair: a colour scheme nobody can choose is a colour scheme that does not exist outside Storybook. It is paired with the language button the owner asked for on the menu bar, and both need the same thing, a preference that survives a reload and is reachable from anywhere, so doing them together is cheaper than doing either alone.
tasks.exit: A user can choose light, dark or system in the running app, the choice survives a reload, an e2e test proves both, and the same mechanism carries the language choice.
notes: ROAST RAISED THIS TWICE, rating it critical both times: main.tsx mounts AppProviders with no preference, so production is permanently light and the whole colour scheme exists only through the Storybook toolbar. Recorded here rather than argued: the reviewer is right that filing a card does not make the provider usable, and the reason it is a card is the loop rule, not a judgement that it does not matter. Also worth carrying into this work: light text/secondary on bg/page is 4.51 to one and the light interview chip is 4.51, both passing by a hair, so a page token that gets slightly lighter breaks them.

tasks.title: The no-raw-value test excludes src/theme, where a component with raw values lives
tasks.desc: src/theme/noLiterals.test.ts skips the whole theme directory, because that is where hexes legitimately live. But Tokens.stories.tsx also lives there and it hardcodes 40, 16 and a 999 radius, which the no-raw-spacing rule forbids. Exclude only the files that are the token source rather than the directory, so a component that happens to sit next to them is still checked. The scan also misses rgb(), hsl() and named CSS colours, MDX, index.html inline styles and CSS files.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major. The exclusion was written as a directory because that was easy, and the first component to sit in that directory is already breaking the rule the test exists to enforce. Every component folder will eventually hold a story next to a helper, so an exclusion by directory is the wrong shape from the start.
tasks.exit: The token modules are excluded by name rather than by directory, Tokens.stories.tsx is scanned and its raw values are gone, the scan also rejects rgb(), hsl() and named colours, and a planted violation in each covered form fails the run.
notes: ROAST CONFIRMED IT A SECOND TIME, in round 2 of KN-005, with the specific values: Tokens.stories.tsx hardcodes 40 and 16 as sizes and 999 as a radius, and lives inside the directory the guard skips, so the guard cannot establish the no-component-file invariant it claims. Not new information, recorded because a finding raised twice is evidence the card matters more than its severity says.

tasks.title: Localise the Storybook toolbar labels, or decide in writing that they stay English
tasks.desc: The Language and Theme toolbars in .storybook/preview.tsx carry bare English strings, Language, Theme, Light, Dark (derived) and System, and the lingui rule does not reach .storybook because that directory is build configuration for a developer tool. Either route them through the catalog so a Persian reviewer sees Persian chrome, or record in AGENTS.md that Storybook chrome is English by decision, with the reason.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major. The done gate asks every change to be reviewed in both languages, and the tool that review happens in is half English either way. It is a small thing that is either fine or not, and the cost of not deciding is that someone re-raises it every few months.
tasks.exit: Either the toolbar labels render from the catalog and a story proves it, or AGENTS.md states that Storybook chrome stays English with the reason and a check keeps product strings out of that directory.

tasks.title: Prove a system colour scheme change actually repaints the tree
tasks.desc: The tests around useSystemScheme register a listener, unregister it and resolve a preference, but nothing dispatches a media query change and then checks the rendered theme followed it. Add a story or a browser test that flips the emulated colour scheme with the preference set to system and asserts the page background changed.
tasks.why: A roast rated this minor and it is the honest gap: what is tested is the plumbing around the subscription, not that the subscription does anything. useSyncExternalStore is exactly the kind of API where a wrong snapshot function still registers a listener and still never updates.
tasks.exit: A test emulates a prefers-color-scheme change with the preference set to system and asserts the rendered background moved from the light value to the dark one, and it fails when the store returns a constant.

tasks.title: Dark destructive controls fail contrast, because on-accent is one token for two fills
tasks.desc: theme.ts gives the single derived text/on-accent to both primary.contrastText and error.contrastText, and darkMode.ts walks that one value against the BRAND background only. On the derived error main it is 3.64 to one and on error hover 4.24, both under 4.5, so a dark destructive button is unreadable while the new contrast suite passes because it only checks blue. Derive a second on-accent for the danger fill, or make the walk take every background a token is used against.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical after recomputing every ratio, and it is the exact shape of the bug the contrast suite was written to catch, one level up: a token checked against one of its backgrounds and used against two. Destructive buttons are the ones where a misread is expensive, and the design has bg/danger/default and hover precisely so a delete looks like a delete.
tasks.exit: Every derived contrastText clears 4.5 to one against every fill the theme pairs it with, a test enumerates those pairs from the theme rather than from a hand-written list, and it fails when a fill changes without its text following.

tasks.title: Move apps/web/src to the folder structure AGENTS.md prescribes
tasks.desc: AGENTS.md fixes the layout as src/core for singletons, src/pages one folder per route, src/shared for components operations types and utils, src/locales for the catalogs, and says only these, with src itself holding App.tsx, main.tsx and the Storybook landing page. What exists is src/app, src/i18n, src/theme and src/gate-fixtures. Move i18n and theme into core, the catalogs into locales, App into src, and decide where gate-fixtures belongs since it is neither a singleton nor shared. Add a check so the next new folder cannot be invented.
tasks.why: The structure was written down before any code existed and the first code ignored it, the same way the import conventions were ignored, and for the same reason: nothing checks. It matters now rather than later because the component queue is about to create thirty folders, and moving thirty is a different job from moving four. It pairs with KN-092, which adds the import lint, since both fixes touch every file.
tasks.exit: Every file under apps/web/src sits in core, pages, shared or locales, or is App.tsx or main.tsx, a check fails when a folder outside that set appears, and the whole gate still passes.

tasks.title: Wire the lingui macro plugin so catalogs are extracted rather than hand written
tasks.desc: Strings go through <Trans id="English sentence" /> and i18n._() with hand-written catalogs in src/i18n/locales. TECH-DEBT entry 8 records why: the macro transform needs @lingui/swc-plugin wired into @vitejs/plugin-react-swc, and that plugin is compiled against a specific swc ABI, so a mismatch fails the build for a reason unrelated to what was being built. Wire it, switch the components to the macro, run lingui extract into po files, and delete the hand-written catalogs.
tasks.why: Message ids are written twice today, once in the JSX and once in the catalog, and only a test keeps them in step. The macro removes the second copy entirely and lingui extract keeps the catalog honest by construction, which is the difference between a rule and a habit. It is filed rather than done because the ABI risk is real and the runtime API already satisfies every clause of KN-006.
tasks.exit: Components use the Trans and t macros with no explicit id, lingui extract produces the catalogs, the hand-written ones are gone, npm test and npm run build both pass, and TECH-DEBT entry 8 is removed.
notes: RAISED AS A CRITICAL TWICE on KN-006, both times on the same ground: the card DESC names the macro plugin and neither vite.config.ts nor either vitest project configures it, there is no lingui.config file and no .po catalog. Recorded rather than argued. The reason it is a card is that KN-006 EXIT condition does not name the macro, only the behaviour, and the behaviour is met and proved end to end; TECH-DEBT entry 8 carries the ABI risk that made it a deferral rather than an oversight. If the owner reads the desc as binding, this card is the work.

tasks.title: Forbid the message-id forms the catalog scan cannot see
tasks.desc: src/i18n/catalog.test.ts finds used ids with two regexes, <Trans id="..."> and i18n._(single or double quoted). <Trans id={"Delete this application"} />, a template literal, an identifier, or a reordered prop list all miss it, so the id never reaches the catalog and a Persian user silently gets the English fallback. Add the lingui rule that requires an explicit literal id, or a rule of our own that rejects a non-literal id, so the scan is sufficient BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by everyone happening to write it the same way.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical. The catalog test is what stands behind the claim that the Persian catalog is 100 percent translated, and a gate that only sees one spelling of a thing is a gate that measures spelling. The failure is silent and reaches the user, which is the worst combination: no error, no test failure, just English text on a Persian screen.
tasks.exit: A Trans with a braced or template-literal id fails npm run lint, a committed fixture holds each form, and the catalog test still finds every id the codebase uses.
notes: RAISED A SECOND TIME in round 2 of KN-006, with two more forms than the card names: <Trans otherProp={x} id="..."> also misses the scan because the regex requires id to follow Trans immediately, and a template literal argument to i18n._ misses it too. The fix is unchanged and it is the right one, forbid the forms the scan cannot see so the scan is sufficient by construction, but the card understated how many forms there are.

tasks.title: Two preference setters called in one batch lose the first update
tasks.desc: PreferencesProvider builds each setter over the locale and colorScheme captured in that render, so setLocale("en-US") followed synchronously by setColorScheme("dark") computes the second update from the stale locale: the state and the stored value both end up {locale: "fa-IR", colorScheme: "dark"} and the language change is gone. Use a functional state update and persist the value the updater computed.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major and it is a plain correctness bug in new code. It is dormant only because there is one control today; the moment the settings surface offers both, a user changing two things at once loses one of them, and the symptom is a preference that sometimes does not stick, which is the hardest kind of bug to believe a report of.
tasks.exit: A test calls both setters in the same batch and both changes survive in the state and in what was written, and it fails against the current closure-based implementation.

roasts.head: 944d888ae8d23ab7ee1c539c836482370a42ed17
roasts.dismissed: One major is rejected in part. The reviewer says the story puts user-facing documentation prose into source including a JSDoc block, violating the documentation contract. AGENTS.md forbids JSDoc above const meta and a docblock above a story export; the block it points at is above clickingBothSetters, a local helper, and it explains why the helper restores storage, which is code explanation and therefore a comment by that document's own test: if it explains the code to whoever edits it, it is a comment. So the placement is not a violation. The other half of that finding, that the story ships no bilingual Story Docs page, is REAL and is exactly KN-158, already filed: AGENTS.md mandates src/shared/story-docs/{en,fa} and a guard test, and none of it exists, no directory, no guard, and all three pre-existing stories carry the JSDoc the rule forbids. Adding the first story-docs page would mean building that system, which is KN-158's work and not a one point bug fix. The reviewer's answer to my ref question is also worth recording: it confirms the fix is correct for the synchronous handler case and correctly objects that my comment's absolute cannot disagree is too broad, since a transition can leave the ref ahead of rendered state without losing either field. Its counter-proposal for the click check, a handler-invocation counter asserted at runtime rather than a regex over the source, is better than what I wrote and is folded into KN-178's exit condition.

tasks.evidence: node agent/scripts/verify/KN-112.mjs passes, 5 checks. Both halves of the exit condition are proved with the instrument each needs. What was WRITTEN is proved in the node project, where renderToString never re-renders so two setter calls hit the same snapshot, observed through a stubbed localStorage. The RENDERED STATE is proved by a story in real headless Chromium whose probe has ONE button calling both setters, because a batch is what an event handler makes and two calls after renderToString returns are not one. The verifier also asserts the story clicks exactly once, since two clicks are two renders and would pass against the defect while still printing a pass. Five mutations were each caught with their own message and every file restored: setColorScheme forwarding the stale locale, which is the original defect and fails BOTH the node test and the browser story, so the exit condition's clause about failing against the closure-based implementation is proved by running it; setLocale forwarding the stale colour scheme; the ref reverted to the render snapshot; the old assertion that enshrined the defect restored; and the story clicking twice. Writing those mutations exposed a gap in my own tests, which is worth recording: they exercised ONE order only, and since only the SECOND call in a batch overwrites anything, a defect in setLocale alone would have gone uncaught forever. A reversed-order test was added and mutation two is caught by that test alone. The suite previously CERTIFIED this bug rather than missing it, expecting the second write to carry the reverted locale, and the verifier now refuses that assertion's return. AGENTS section 5 items 1 to 4 are green: lint clean, tsc clean, 15 files and 228 tests passing at the 100 percent coverage thresholds, build and Storybook build both succeeded. Item 6, the four language and theme combinations, is honestly PARTIAL: both stories run in fa-IR and en-US, but the probe renders unstyled spans and a label-less button with no token, spacing or direction-dependent layout, so light against dark distinguishes nothing on it. What this does NOT establish: setColorScheme has no production caller today and DESIGN.md draws no settings surface, so this repairs a latent contract defect rather than a reachable user-facing bug, and the probe is currently the only thing in the repository that calls both setters.

tasks.title: Prove the portalled menu anchors correctly in RTL
tasks.desc: LanguageSwitch renders a MUI Menu, which portals out of the tree. The stories assert the items, their text and the accessible name, and never the geometry: nothing checks that the popover anchors to the right edge under direction rtl, which is the one thing a portal is most likely to get wrong because it renders outside the element that carries the direction. Assert the anchor position, or the computed direction on the portalled node, in both directions.
tasks.why: A roast rated this minor and it is the design contract rather than a nicety: RTL is achieved with direction rtl and natural order, and a popover that escapes that is the classic way a right-to-left layout half works. Every component after this one that opens a menu or a dialog inherits whatever this proves.
tasks.exit: A story asserts the menu is anchored to the right of its trigger in RTL and to the left in LTR, and it fails when the direction is not propagated to the portal.

tasks.title: The catalog test counts an empty string as a translation
tasks.desc: src/i18n/catalog.test.ts checks that every used id is a KEY in both catalogs and rejects only a Persian value exactly equal to its English id. Set a Persian message to the empty string and every test still passes, while the user sees nothing at all where a label should be. Reject empty and whitespace-only values, and reject a value that is the English id with punctuation changed, which is the next spelling of the same evasion.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical and it is the clause the whole test exists for: the exit condition says the fa-IR catalog is 100 percent translated and a test fails when it is not, and an empty string is not a translation. An empty label is also worse than an English one, because English text tells a Persian user the string was missed and a blank tells them nothing.
tasks.exit: Setting any Persian message to an empty or whitespace-only string fails npm test and the failure names the id; so does setting one to its English id with the punctuation or casing changed, which is the next spelling of the same evasion and is named in this card's description; each is proved by planting it and watching the suite go red rather than by reading the checks.
notes: Exit condition widened before building, on the plan check's point that the description asked for the punctuation case and the exit condition did not, so the implementation would have been stronger than the contract with nothing recording why.
tasks.evidence: node agent/scripts/verify/KN-114.mjs passes, 10 checks, and it is itself the mutation harness rather than a scratch file thrown away, which is what KN-136 asks for. It plants seven values into the REAL fa-IR catalog and requires the suite to go red NAMING the id for each: an empty string, spaces only, a tab only, a non-breaking space only, zero-width characters only, the English id exactly, and the id lowercased with punctuation added. It plants into the real catalog rather than a copy because the test imports the locale module directly, so a copy in a temp directory would prove the plant was written and not that the suite sees it, which the plan check named as the step most likely to be got wrong. A positive control runs first, since every other check asserts a FAILURE and a suite red for an unrelated reason would satisfy all of them, and a final run after restore proves the plants left nothing behind. Four further mutations weakening the CHECKS were each caught with their own message: the blank check removed, the blank check no longer stripping format characters, the untranslated check reverted to exact equality, and the untranslated check no longer casefolding. Gate: lint clean, tsc clean, 15 files and 229 tests at the 100 percent thresholds, build succeeded. Two things found while building, both corrected: my first blank check used LITERAL zero-width characters in its regex, invisible to any reader, and a comment of mine claimed U+200C is whitespace when it is not, since it is a letter-joining control that appears inside Persian words; the check now strips the Unicode FORMAT category by name and the verifier asserts no invisible character survives in that file. The card's exit condition was WIDENED before building, on the plan check's point that the description asked for the punctuation case while the exit condition covered only empty and whitespace, so the implementation would have been stronger than the contract with nothing recording why. What this does NOT establish: the catalog has three messages and none was blank, so this is preventive rather than a repair, and a Persian value of x still passes, because requiring a Persian character would false-positive on numbers, URLs and proper nouns and the card did not ask for it.

tasks.title: The language names bypass the catalog entirely
tasks.desc: src/i18n/index.ts holds locales as a plain object mapping fa-IR to the raw Persian string and en-US to English, and LanguageSwitch renders those values directly. They are user-facing strings in a .ts file that never go through lingui, which is the rule the whole gate exists for, and the lingui rule does not see them because it is a value in an object rather than a JSX literal. The RENDERED text must stay native, a reader who cannot read the current language has to find their own, but that is an argument about which translation to show, not an argument for having no catalog entry.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major and the distinction is the right one: the self-naming exception explains why the text is not translated, it does not explain why it is invisible to the catalog. As written, the two strings a language switch shows are the only user-facing strings in the product that nothing checks.
tasks.exit: The language names come from the catalog with each locale name present in both catalogs as its own native spelling, the lingui rule sees them, and a missing one fails the catalog test.

tasks.title: Move the language switch out of the placeholder shell into the drawn chrome
tasks.desc: LanguageSwitch currently renders in App.tsx under the placeholder heading, with the sidebar placement on every breakpoint. DESIGN.md puts it at the bottom of the sidebar 185:11 on desktop and in the Page Header 155:56 as a trailing action on mobile, and says nothing else moves. Move it when those exist, choose the placement responsively, and delete the temporary block and its comment from App.tsx.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major and it is right that the shell placement is not one of the two approved homes. It was put there deliberately, because a control only Storybook renders cannot show that a choice persists, and because the shell is itself a placeholder rather than a drawn frame, so nothing drawn is being reflowed. That reasoning expires the moment the sidebar exists.
tasks.exit: The switch renders at the bottom of the sidebar on desktop and as a Page Header trailing action on mobile, App.tsx contains no language control, and an e2e test finds it in both places at the two drawn viewports.

tasks.title: Re-triage severity, because 78 of 105 open cards are high
tasks.desc: The selection law orders by severity, then points, then id. 78 of the 105 open tasks are high, 3 are critical, 21 medium and 3 low, so severity has stopped discriminating and the law is effectively picking by points and id. Most of the high ones arrived from roasts, where high was the honest rating of a finding in isolation and is not its rating against the other 77. Re-rate the board against a written definition of each level, and add that definition to AGENTS.md so the next fifty findings do not repeat it.
tasks.why: The whole point of the law is that the script picks rather than the author, and a board where four fifths of the work shares one severity hands the choice back to whoever wrote the points. It also hides the genuinely urgent: three criticals are invisible in a list of seventy-eight highs. Found by looking at the distribution rather than at any one card.
tasks.exit: AGENTS.md defines each severity with a test a card can be held to, no level holds more than half the open board, and npm run todo -- validate reports the distribution so the next drift is visible.

tasks.title: Health says ok while the database is unreachable, and the URLs are only checked for emptiness
tasks.desc: src/config/env.ts requires DATABASE_URL and WEB_ORIGIN to be non-empty strings and nothing more, so DATABASE_URL=not-a-postgres-url and WEB_ORIGIN=not a URL both start the service. Nothing connects to the database at any point, so the health query answers ok against a database that does not exist. Validate both as URLs with the schemes they must have, and make health a readiness check that reports the database separately from the process.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major twice over and it is the deploy failure this whole config file was written to prevent, one level deeper: the point of requiring DATABASE_URL before listening is that a server which starts without a database and fails on the first query is worse than one that refuses to start. As written it starts and then reports itself healthy, which is the same failure with a green light on it.
tasks.exit: A malformed DATABASE_URL or WEB_ORIGIN fails at startup and names which, the health query reports the database separately from the process, and it does not say ok when the database cannot be reached, proved against a URL pointing at a closed port.

tasks.title: Nothing tests CORS, the port binding or the startup path
tasks.desc: vitest.config.ts excludes src/main.ts from coverage, which is where CORS is configured, the port is bound and the CLI failure path lives. So the 100 percent figure is reported over a file set that omits the only code a deploy actually depends on, and a change to the allowed origin, to credentials, or to origin: true would keep the gate green. Export the parts of bootstrap that can be tested without listening, test the CORS options object directly, and add a preflight test against the running server in the probe.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major. The excluded file is not an uninteresting one: origin: true instead of the configured value is the difference between a CORS policy and the absence of one, and it is a one-word edit that nothing would catch. The exclusion was written for the right reason, main.ts starts a real server, and the wrong conclusion was drawn from it.
tasks.exit: A preflight from an unexpected origin does not receive that origin back, a test covers the CORS options and the port resolution without binding a port, main.ts is no longer excluded from coverage wholesale, and changing origin to true fails the run.

tasks.title: Make schema.gql a checked build artefact rather than a side effect of starting the server
tasks.desc: autoSchemaFile writes schema.gql to process.cwd() when the application boots, and the file is gitignored. npm run build runs tsc only, so a fresh clone has no schema, and packages/graphql is supposed to generate the client types from it. That means the contract between the two halves can only be regenerated by someone able to boot the server with a full environment and a writable directory, and nothing can fail a build because the schema changed and the client types did not. Generate it in a build step, commit it, and add a check that the committed file matches what the resolvers produce.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major and it is the load bearing one for everything after: KN-035 generates types from this file both ways, and a generated artefact that is neither committed nor reproducible is a contract nobody can diff. The one thing a code-first schema is for is that the server cannot disagree with the client, and that only holds if the file is checked.
tasks.exit: npm run build produces schema.gql without starting a server, the file is committed, and a check fails when the resolvers and the committed schema disagree.

roasts.head: 2c6aa3d48f48c2fa867061d37d442600f2e11c6c
roasts.dismissed: The first critical is a real observation and not a defect to fix. The exit condition says npm run build produces schema.gql; the build now CHECKS it and schema:update produces it. Making build produce it is what round 1 correctly called critical, because a build that regenerates the artefact before comparing it destroys the evidence it is supposed to reject, and the third clause of the same exit condition, that a check fails when the resolvers and the committed schema disagree, cannot hold at the same time. The two clauses are contradictory as written. I have taken the third, which is the one with the guarantee in it, and said so in the evidence rather than quietly rewriting the first. The substance of the first clause, that the schema can be produced without starting a server, is met by schema:update and is verified with an empty environment.

notes: RAISED TO CRITICAL because it blocks one. KN-035, the codegen, generates the client types from schema.gql, so a schema that is gitignored and only appears when the server boots makes that card impossible to do honestly. The board refused to record the dependency while this was merely high, on the grounds that a blocker less severe than what it blocks never gets picked first, which is the right refusal and is why this is now critical rather than why the dependency was dropped.
tasks.evidence: The schema is a committed, tracked file, produced by npm run schema:update from the same decorators the server reads, with no server, no environment and no database: the verifier compiles and generates with WEB_ORIGIN, DATABASE_URL and PORT all absent. The server builds its schema in memory now, so starting it in the wrong directory can no longer rewrite the contract. A stale schema fails the ORDINARY build, proved by appending a type nobody wrote and running npm run build, which is the clause that matters and the one round 1 found false. Nine checks pass, and six planted mutations were caught: re-ignoring the file, putting generation back on the boot path, removing the check from the build, making the comparison always return equal, deleting the sentence that says how to fix it, and emptying the resolver list. One clause is NOT met as literally worded, and I would rather say so than rewrite it. The card says npm run build produces schema.gql; it checks it, and schema:update produces it. Making the build produce it is exactly what round 1 rated critical, because a build that regenerates the artefact before comparing destroys the evidence it should reject, and the third clause of the same condition, that a check fails when the resolvers and the committed schema disagree, cannot hold at the same time. The two clauses contradict each other; I took the one carrying the guarantee. What else this does NOT establish, both filed: nothing asserts there is exactly one graphql in the tree, which is the unmeasured half of the two-project Vitest workaround recorded as TECH-DEBT 10, KN-126; and the check that the generator and the application share one list reads source text, so a resolver default-exported from a file not named *.resolver.ts and registered with a space before the colon reaches the server without reaching the schema while everything stays green, KN-127, now high with the reviewer exact bypasses on it.

tasks.title: Remove the escape hatches in the API tests, and the comment that denies them
tasks.desc: src/health/health.resolver.test.ts casts a fake object through unknown to ConfigService twice, and src/config/env.test.ts carries an eslint-disable for no-dynamic-delete with a cast beside it and no TECH-DEBT entry. AGENTS.md bans both, and TECH-DEBT is where anything suppressed is supposed to be recorded. Worse, a comment in health.test.ts says an `as` there "would be the first one in the repository", which was already false when it was written. Build a real ConfigService or a typed stub that satisfies the contract, drop the disable, and correct the comment.
tasks.why: A roast rated these minor and they are, individually. Together they are the pattern the whole ban exists to stop: a cast in a test masks whether the mock satisfies the dependency it stands in for, so the test passes and the wiring is unproven. And a comment asserting the rule is kept, in a file next to two violations of it, is the thing that makes the next reader stop checking.
tasks.exit: No `as` and no eslint-disable under apps/api, the resolver test uses a stub the type system accepts on its own, and the claim in health.test.ts is true or gone.

tasks.title: Prettier is named in the API scaffold and is in neither the scripts nor the gate
tasks.desc: The KN-033 card says the scaffold includes Prettier. apps/api has no format or format:check script, the root .prettierrc is never applied to it by any command, and agent/scripts/verify/KN-033.mjs does not run it. A badly formatted API file passes every gate. Add the script, add it to the verifier, and do the same for apps/web, which has the same gap.
tasks.why: A roast rated this minor. It matters slightly more than it looks because the web workspace has the same hole, so nothing in this repository actually enforces formatting anywhere, while both cards claim it. A formatter that is configured and never run is a configuration file pretending to be a rule.
tasks.exit: npm run format:check fails on a deliberately misformatted file in each workspace, and both KN-003 and KN-033 verifiers run it.

tasks.title: The migration runner has no transaction, no lock, no failure state and no checksum
tasks.desc: src/database/migrations.ts runs each migration and writes its ledger row as separate statements. A migration that fails halfway leaves partial DDL with no ledger row, so the next deploy replays it and fails permanently on the CREATE TYPE that already exists. Two runners racing can both see "not applied". An applied migration edited afterwards is silently skipped, because nothing records a checksum. Wrap each migration and its ledger row in one transaction, take an advisory lock for the run, record a failed state rather than nothing, and store a checksum that is compared on every deploy.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical and named the exact sequence. It is the single thing here most likely to cost real data: the first time a migration fails against Supabase, the retry makes it worse rather than better, and the recovery is manual SQL against a production database. Prisma migrate deploy solves all four and the runner exists only because Prisma 7 wants a live database at generate time, which is a smaller problem than this one.
tasks.exit: A migration that throws halfway leaves the database unchanged and the ledger recording a failure, a second concurrent run waits rather than racing, an applied migration whose SQL changed fails the next deploy by checksum, and each of those is proved by a planted case against PGlite.
notes: Measured against PGlite before designing, rather than assumed. (1) pg_try_advisory_lock works and is re-entrant within a session, so the lock is real and testable. (2) DDL IS transactional: a ROLLBACK undid a CREATE TYPE, so wrapping each migration with its ledger row in one transaction genuinely gives the atomicity the exit condition asks for. (3) A failed statement inside BEGIN leaves the session ABORTED and every later statement fails with 'current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block', so the runner must issue an explicit ROLLBACK on failure or it poisons the connection and the failure that follows names the wrong cause. That is the trap in the failure-state clause. (4) Two PGlite instances cannot share a dataDir, so the concurrency clause cannot be proved with two real runners; prove it by asserting the lock is requested before any migration runs and that a runner told the lock is held waits rather than proceeding.

Second probe, the transaction mechanics themselves. exec() of a single BEGIN + migration + ledger-INSERT + COMMIT string DOES throw the real error ('relation kn123_ok already exists'), so the runner can detect the failure rather than having to inspect state afterwards. The partial DDL was rolled back CLEANLY, nothing left behind, which is the atomicity clause proved on the engine before writing a line of it. An explicit ROLLBACK restores the session; without one the next statement dies with 'current transaction is aborted'. So the order in the catch is forced and is not a style choice: ROLLBACK first, then write the failure row, then rethrow. Also settled: pg_advisory_lock BLOCKS, and a deploy that hangs forever is worse than one that fails, so use pg_try_advisory_lock with a bounded retry and an error that says another deploy is migrating. And the ledger's own ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS runs outside the lock on first deploy, which is idempotent so two racing runners both succeed; that deserves a comment rather than a fix.

fixedSince.head: 19d5525bbccd43605c2cb2c39fe186e4b613df9f
fixedSince.why: Round 4's two criticals were data-loss paths and both were fixed in place: identifier boundaries are Unicode-aware, so a non-ASCII name no longer lets a dollar quote swallow an ABORT, and a line comment now ends at a bare carriage return as well as a newline. Each carries the reviewer's exact reproduction as a regression test. The harness also gained two regressions covering those fixes and was made twelve minutes faster. The round still stands: nothing it examined was removed, everything it asked for was added, and its remaining findings are filed as KN-146 and KN-147.

tasks.evidence:
The migration runner had four defects, each a way to cost a production database. All four are closed and each is proved by planting the case against PGlite, Postgres compiled to wasm running in process, so the SQL is executed by the engine Supabase runs.

ONE TRANSACTION. The migration SQL and its ledger row go in a single statement batch. The first version issued two separate exec calls, so a migration could commit with nothing recording it and the next deploy would replay it and die on a CREATE TYPE that already existed. A recording runner asserts the batch containing the DDL also contains the ledger INSERT. The assertion is about ONE BATCH rather than about the BEGIN keyword for a reason: the harness first planted removal of the explicit BEGIN and the suite stayed GREEN, because Postgres wraps a multi-statement simple query in an implicit transaction, so the test as first written was measuring Postgres rather than this code.

A RUN LOCK, pg_try_advisory_lock with bounded retries rather than pg_advisory_lock, because a deploy that hangs forever is worse than one that fails. Taken BEFORE the ledger DDL: the earlier order carried a comment claiming two racing runners would both succeed because every statement was idempotent, which is false, CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is not race safe.

A RECORDED FAILURE, applied_at NULL, failed_at set, error text stored. ROLLBACK comes first in the catch and that order is forced: a failed statement leaves the session aborted and every later statement dies with 'current transaction is aborted' until the rollback.

A CHECKSUM, sha256 of the SQL, compared every deploy, so an applied migration edited afterwards is refused rather than silently skipped. A row predating the column is adopted so an existing database still deploys; that limitation is KN-144.

The transaction guard is a left-to-right scanner: line comments ended by EITHER terminator, nested block comments, ordinary and E-strings, doubled-quote escapes, quoted identifiers, and tagged or untagged dollar quotes with Unicode-aware identifier boundaries. Four roast rounds found six holes and every one is a regression test now: inline COMMIT, ABORT and END; a command between two strings that look like dollar quotes; ABORT split by a block comment, which Postgres reads as ABORT WORK; and transaction control after a dollar sign inside an ASCII and then a non-ASCII identifier.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. The scanner is a screen, not a proof. Six holes found the same way says there is a seventh, so KN-146 replaces it with a structural check that never reads the SQL: a temp table ON COMMIT DROP with the ledger INSERT conditioned on it, so an early COMMIT or ABORT cannot write a success row whatever syntax produced it. Defence in depth rather than a live bug, because Prisma generates these migrations and never emits transaction control. KN-147 covers the last finding, that nothing proves the runner WAITS between lock attempts.

agent/scripts/verify/KN-123.mjs IS the mutation harness, committed rather than thrown away, which is what KN-136 asks for generally. It removes each of fifteen guarantees in turn and requires the suite to fail through the named test. It now runs each planted case against only that test, so the verify takes three minutes rather than eighteen, and it refuses a run whose filter matched no test at all, because that exits non-zero too and would otherwise look like a catch.

Gate: lint clean, lint:tsc clean, 67 database tests passing, 100 percent statements and branches, verify passing in 3m04s. Nothing renders, so AGENTS.md section 5 steps 5 to 7 were not performed and are not claimed.

Four rounds, 5.0, 5.0, 4.0, 4.0, seven criticals, every one real and every one a path to a migration recorded APPLIED that never ran. Filed rather than fixed: KN-143, KN-144, KN-145, KN-146, KN-147, KN-148.

tasks.title: Status history is documented as immutable and nothing enforces it
tasks.desc: The schema comment says history is appended and never rewritten, and the verifier checks that StatusHistory has no updatedAt. Neither stops anything: the application role can UPDATE or DELETE rows in status_history like any other table. Enforce it, with a rule or a trigger that rejects UPDATE and DELETE except through the cascade from its job record, or with a role that lacks those grants, and change the comment to describe what is enforced rather than what is intended.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical. The trail is the product: DESIGN.md says the value is the trail rather than the listing, so a history table anyone can edit is the one table where a silent write is worth catching. The absence of an updatedAt column is a statement about intent that reads like a guarantee, which is the kind of claim this repository has been wrong about before.
tasks.exit: An UPDATE or a DELETE against status_history is rejected by the database, deleting a job record still removes its history through the cascade, and both are proved against PGlite.

tasks.title: The seed builds SQL by concatenation and several values skip the quote helper
tasks.desc: src/database/seed.ts has a quote helper that doubles apostrophes, and the note, the contacts, the feedback body, the user name and the phone are interpolated as raw literals instead. Nothing in the current data contains an apostrophe, so it works; a contact named O Brien or a feedback body containing we are, spelled with the apostrophe, breaks the statement. Doubling apostrophes is also only correct while standard_conforming_strings is on. Use parameters rather than interpolation throughout.
tasks.why: A roast rated this minor and it is, until someone edits the seed. The failure is a syntax error from Postgres pointing at generated SQL, which is a bad ten minutes for whoever is just trying to add a row. Parameters remove the whole class rather than the current instance.
tasks.exit: Every value the seed writes goes through a parameter rather than into the SQL text, a seeded record containing an apostrophe and a backslash round trips intact, and the quote helper is gone.

tasks.title: Assert there is exactly one graphql in the dependency tree
tasks.desc: apps/api/vitest.config.ts runs two projects because graphql and @nestjs/graphql need opposite inlining under Vite, recorded as TECH-DEBT entry 10. The split is a test-runner workaround and is not evidence that production is safe: if a future dependency ever pulls a second physical copy of graphql, the built server hits the same identity failure at schema construction, which is startup rather than a request. Add npm ls graphql, or an equivalent, to the API verifier and fail when more than one version resolves.
tasks.why: A roast raised it as the unmeasured half of a workaround it otherwise accepted. The failure is loud rather than silent, which is the good news, but it happens at boot on a deploy rather than in a test, and the check that would catch it in advance is one command.
tasks.exit: agent/scripts/verify/KN-033.mjs fails when more than one graphql version resolves, proved by a planted duplicate, and TECH-DEBT entry 10 names it as the check that retires the split.

tasks.title: The resolver-registration check reads text rather than the container
tasks.desc: src/graphql/schema.test.ts proves the generator and the application share one list by grepping graphql.module.ts for providers: [...resolvers] and grepping other module files for a stray Resolver provider. That misses a resolver in a file not named *.resolver.ts, a default export, a re-export under another name, and a resolver registered through a dynamic module. Ask NEST instead: build the application context and compare the resolvers it actually instantiated against the generated schema fields.
tasks.why: A roast rated the previous version of this critical because the two lists were genuinely separate, and they are one list now, which is the important half. What is left is that the CHECK is a text scan standing in for a runtime fact, and a text scan is what let the first version look fine. The application context already boots in the health test, so asking it is cheap.
tasks.exit: A resolver registered in a way the text scan cannot see, a default export in a file not named *.resolver.ts, is detected, and the check reads the resolvers from a booted Nest context rather than from source text.
notes: ROUND 2 GAVE THE EXACT BYPASSES, and they are worse than the card said. The guard requires the literal text "providers:" so "providers : [ExtraResolver]" with a space walks past it; it only reads *.module.ts, so a module defined anywhere else is invisible; and the companion scan only reads *.resolver.ts and only matches "export class Name", so a default-exported resolver in src/extra.ts is missed by both. The reviewer constructed the case: a resolver registered from an imported module gains its fields in the running server while generation, npm test and npm run build all pass. That is the single-source-of-truth claim failing in the direction that matters, a field the server answers and the contract does not carry. Reading the booted Nest container instead of the source text closes all four at once, which is why this is one card rather than four patches to a regex.

tasks.title: Generate typed GraphQL operations instead of asserting them by hand
tasks.desc: HEAD_QUERY is a gql template with a hand-written TypedDocumentNode annotation, and HealthQueryData is Pick<Query, health>. Neither is generated or validated against the schema. Misspell a selected field, environmentTypo, and TypeScript accepts it because the annotation was asserted rather than derived, and the server rejects the request at runtime. The declared response type also claims the whole Health object rather than the three fields selected, so adding a required field to Health makes the type say Apollo returned something the query never asked for. The typescript-operations plugin is installed and unused; switch to generated operation types, or the client preset, so the document and its type come from the same place.
tasks.why: A roast rated this critical and it is the card own why: the reason for a monorepo is that a schema change fails at typecheck rather than at runtime, and the one place that guarantee is exercised is the place it does not hold. A misspelled field is the most common GraphQL mistake there is, and it currently reaches production silently.
tasks.exit: A query selecting a field that does not exist fails the build, the response type reflects the SELECTION rather than the whole object type, adding a required field to Health does not change HealthQueryData, and each is proved by a planted case.
tasks.evidence:
The operation lives in packages/graphql/src/operations/health.graphql, where codegen validates it against apps/api/schema.gql at generation time. typescript-operations and typed-document-node emit HealthDocument and HealthQuery together so a consumer cannot pair the wrong two, and apps/web/src/core/api/health.ts re-exports them instead of holding a gql template with a hand-written TypedDocumentNode annotation.

Exit condition, clause by clause, each proved by planting the case. A query selecting a field that does not exist fails the build: a field in the operation is misspelled and the ROOT build must refuse with the diagnostic naming the field and the type, not merely a failed build, so the refusal is codegen comparing document to schema rather than something incidental. The response type is the SELECTION: HealthQuery is an inline shape of the three selected fields and the check refuses any mention of the Health object type. Adding a REQUIRED field to Health does not change it: a non-null field is added to the model and supplied in the resolver, the API recompiles, schema.gql and the types regenerate, the emitted SDL is asserted to carry that field as non-null so the plant cannot regress to nullable under the required clause's name, and then the query type must be byte-identical AND a probe reading the new field through the web consumer must fail with exactly one TS2339 naming it. Byte equality alone was not enough: the hand-written whole-object shape this card removed has text that does not change when Health gains a field either.

The verifier writes and restores. It snapshots the five files it can touch before any check runs, refuses to start if anything already occupies the probe path, and the closing check compares bytes against those snapshots rather than running the build, because the plant is internally consistent by construction so a run that restored nothing still builds. Twenty mutations planted and twenty caught, including the two that earlier versions missed: a probe importing the generated file rather than the consumer, and the whole-object Query type aliased under the right name. Those cases live in a scratch directory rather than the repository, which the reviewer twice declined to certify and was right to; that is filed as KN-136.

Gate: root lint clean, lint:tsc clean, 286 tests passing at 100 percent statements, branches, functions and lines across apps/web and apps/api, build succeeds with both schema.gql and generated.ts reported as matching. AGENTS.md section 5 steps 5 to 7 were NOT performed and are not claimed: nothing renders this module yet, so there is no story or screen to open in fa-IR and en-US, light and dark.

Six roast rounds: 7.0, 8.0, then 9.0 four times, zero criticals from round 2 on. Round 6 answered every clause of the exit condition yes and found no new defect. Four of those rounds should not have happened. Rounds 3 to 5 were fixes that the loop's mechanical test says should have been cards, and round 6 was the cost of attaching the verify command after the roast rather than before, which changes the card digest. Both mistakes are filed: the ordering trap as KN-139, and round 5's two real findings as KN-137 the verifier checks the exported type but never the exported document, and KN-138 it attributes compiler errors by substring rather than by path. The fixes already written for those were reverted so this closes on the state that was actually reviewed.

tasks.title: The duplicate-type scan only sees exported top-level declarations
tasks.desc: packages/graphql/src/handwritten.test.ts finds a duplicate only when it is a top-level export whose name exactly matches a generated type. A local interface LocalHealth with the same three fields, or an unexported interface Health inside a module, is invisible and can stand in for the generated type throughout a file. Compare SHAPES rather than names, or use the type checker: a declaration structurally identical to a generated type is the duplicate, whatever it is called.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major. The clause is that no hand-written interface duplicates a generated one, and a scan matching names catches only the honest case: someone who writes LocalJobRecord to avoid the import is exactly the person the rule is for. Name matching also produces the wrong error for the right problem.
tasks.exit: A local, unexported interface structurally identical to a generated type is detected in the web app, a differently named one is too, and an unrelated interface with some overlapping fields is not.

tasks.title: The no-data health reason is English copy outside the catalog
tasks.desc: apps/web/src/core/api/health.ts returns { kind: down, reason: the API answered with nothing } when the response has no data and no error. That is user-facing English produced in a core module, in the same file whose comment says user-facing text must not originate there, so a Persian user sees English on exactly the failure that is hardest to explain. The lingui rule did not catch it because reason also carries network messages, which are not ours. Separate the two: a code the component translates, and a passthrough for whatever the network said.
tasks.why: A roast rated this major and the sharpest part is that the comment beside it claims the opposite. A file that states a rule and breaks it in the next function is worse than one that does neither, because the next reader believes the comment.
tasks.exit: No English sentence originates in apps/web/src/core, the empty-response case carries a code the component renders through the catalog, a network message still passes through untranslated, and the catalog test covers the new id.

tasks.title: Make the root build typecheck what it ships
tasks.desc: apps/web/package.json build is "vite build" and nothing else. Vite transpiles per file and never typechecks, so the only typecheck of the web app is the separate "lint:tsc" script. npm run build therefore compiles and emits a bundle whose types were never verified. Concrete sequence found by a roast on KN-128: remove a selected field from packages/graphql/src/operations/health.graphql, regenerate, and run npm run build. Both generation checks agree because both sides regenerated, but nothing typechecks apps/web/src/core/api/health.ts, which still reads input.data.health.environment. The build passes and toHealthState returns { kind: 'up', environment: undefined }, which reaches the screen. Add typechecking to the web build, and check whether the API and graphql workspace builds have the same hole.
tasks.why: npm run build is the command a deploy runs, and KN-051 will wire it to GitHub Pages. A build that does not typecheck what it emits is a deploy that ships a type error as a blank field. This is the same class as KN-120, where the build regenerated the artefact before comparing and therefore always passed: a gate that cannot fail is not a gate.
tasks.exit: Removing a selected field from the health operation and regenerating makes npm run build fail, proved by planting exactly that, and the failure names the consumer file rather than something incidental. Every workspace build either typechecks its own sources or the verifier records why it cannot.
tasks.evidence:
apps/web's build was 'vite build' and nothing else. Vite transpiles per file and never typechecks, so npm run build, the command a deploy runs and the one KN-051 is about to point GitHub Pages at, emitted a bundle whose types nothing had verified. packages/graphql was the same shape: codegen:check alone compares generated output byte for byte and never compiles it. apps/api already typechecked, because tsc -p tsconfig.build.json is a compile. Both now run tsc.

Exit condition, both clauses, each proved by planting. Removing a selected field from packages/graphql/src/operations/health.graphql and regenerating now fails the build: the verifier does exactly that, confirms the regenerated response type no longer carries the field so the two halves genuinely agree and nothing is stale, and requires the failure to name apps/web/src/core/api/health.ts and the field. The reviewer reproduced it independently and got TS2339 at health.ts line 47. Every workspace build typechecks its own sources: a type error is appended to a real source file in each of the three workspaces in turn and THAT WORKSPACE'S OWN build must reject it, named.

The per-workspace part is the correction round 1 forced and it was not cosmetic. The first version ran the ROOT build for each plant, and apps/web resolves @karnama/graphql to that package's TypeScript source, so web's compiler reports an error planted in packages/graphql and the root build fails whether or not the graphql build checks anything. Setting the graphql build to 'tsc --noEmit --noCheck' passed both checks. The predicate now rejects --noCheck, and a mutation that puts the plants back on the root build SURVIVES undetected, which is the direct evidence the change carries the clause rather than decorating it.

Eleven mutations across the two rounds, all behaving as predicted, including the operation reduced but NOT regenerated so the build fails as stale rather than over the consumer, which is the distinction the whole check rests on.

Gate: root lint clean, lint:tsc clean, 286 tests passing at 100 percent on all four metrics in apps/web and apps/api, build succeeds. AGENTS.md section 5 steps 5 to 7 were NOT performed and are not claimed: this card changes build scripts and renders nothing.

Two roast rounds, 8.0 both, zero criticals.
